newsitem.title: UK: British defuse N.Irish car bomb in Londonderry.
newsitem.headline: British defuse N.Irish car bomb in Londonderry.

text.p: British army experts defused a huge car bomb left by dissident Irish republican guerrillas outside police headquarters in Northern Ireland's second city, Londonderry, on Thursday.
A caller claiming to speak for the hardline Irish Continuity Army Council rang local news media warning that a saloon car parked outside the base contained a 600lb (275 kilos) device.

"An army technical officer has successfully defused a large car bomb outside Strand Road police station," a Royal Ulster Constabulary police spokesman told Reuters by telephone after a four-hour alert in central Londonderry, a mostly Catholic city.
Hundreds of shoppers and students in surrounding buildings were evacuated as bomb disposal experts examined the suspect car. Experts detonated at least one controlled explosion, eye-witnesses said.
The Britih Broadcasting Corporation said that bomb disposal officers used a robot to set off the controlled explosion and remove bags of explosives.
It was the second major alert within a week in the predominantly Catholic city which like other parts of the province has enjoyed a rare peace for two years.
The incident cast a pall over hopes of an early end to guerrilla violence that has hurt the British-ruled province for 27 years.

The main guerrilla force fighting British rule, the outlawed Irish Republican Army, abandoned a 17-month truce in February with bombs in England and two at military bases in Germany and Northern Ireland.
Last Saturday British forces thwarted what they suspected was a planned landmine attack by the IRA.
Security and political analysts said the emergence of the Irish Continuity Army Council had added a new and destabilising twist to tentative peace efforts.
The IRA has not struck in the province since October 7 when it set off two car bombs in the heart of Britain's military garrison at Lisburn, south of Belfast, killing one soldier and wounding 30.

The IRA claimed responsibility for the Lisburn attack following an earlier claim by the Continuity Army. The absence of IRA hostilities had fuelled speculation that its Sinn Fein political arm and the British government might be edging towards agreement on a new guerrilla truce which would ease the way for Sinn Fein to take its place in all-party talks.
The hawkish Irish Continuity Army Council emerged after the IRA first declared a truce in September 1994.
It blew up a hotel in the west of the province in July, injuring 17, when the region was embroiled in a bout of vicious sectarian violence and staged at least one abortive carbomb attack in Belfast.
Security sources believe its tiny membership broke with the IRA several years ago in protest at moves to politicise the 80-year-old armed campaign by republicans against British forces.
Britain and Ireland are sponsoring multi-party talks with most of the main Northern Ireland parties to try to find a new accord between the two communities.
The majority Protestants support continued British rule but the minority Catholics want unity with neighbouring Catholic Ireland to form a new all-island state ruled from Dublin.
Loyalist guerrillas who waged a battle to defend British rule has maintained a truce for two years, earning their political wings seats in the multi-party talks.
